questions.q: In the hub-and-spoke model, what happens when a new system joins an integration landscape that already uses a middleware hub?
options: It needs a new connection to every existing system, same as point-to-point
It needs N-1 new connections, where N is the number of existing systems
It cannot join unless the hub is rebuilt from scratch
It needs exactly one new connection — to the hub — rather than a connection to each existing system
questions.explain: Hub-and-spoke turns connection growth linear: each system, including a new one, connects once to the central hub, rather than needing a direct connection to every other system as point-to-point would require.

questions.q: What is iPaaS, as distinct from older on-premises middleware like a traditional ESB?
options: iPaaS is a synonym for point-to-point integration
iPaaS is cloud-hosted, subscription middleware with pre-built connectors and visual flow design, so the customer doesn't install, patch, or scale the infrastructure themselves
iPaaS only works with Salesforce and no other platform
iPaaS eliminates the need for any error handling or retry logic
questions.explain: iPaaS is the cloud-native evolution of middleware: a vendor-hosted platform with pre-built connectors and visual flow tools, so the integration team configures flows instead of maintaining the underlying infrastructure.

questions.q: How does this lesson say an architect should treat MuleSoft within the Salesforce Architect exam and practice context?
options: As a tool to be mastered hands-on before anything else in the integration curriculum
As a deprecated product no longer relevant to Salesforce architecture
As a platform an architect should understand conceptually — what it's for and where it fits in a hub-and-spoke design — without necessarily building Mule flows directly
As the only acceptable integration tool for any Salesforce project
questions.explain: This course treats MuleSoft conceptually: an architect is expected to know what it's for and how it fits into an integration landscape (typically in the hub position), not to have hands-on Mule development skill as part of this curriculum.

questions.q: Select the real cost of introducing a middleware or iPaaS layer that this lesson names.
options: It adds at least one extra network hop compared to a direct point-to-point call, which matters for latency-sensitive flows
It eliminates the need to secure any integration endpoint
It guarantees zero downtime for every connected system
It removes the need for an interface contract between systems
questions.explain: Routing a request through middleware adds at least one more network round-trip than calling the target system directly — a real latency cost that matters most for latency-sensitive integrations.

questions.q: Why does this lesson describe introducing middleware as a deliberate trade-off rather than an automatic upgrade?
options: Because middleware is universally cheaper than point-to-point in every scenario
Because middleware is only legal to use in regulated industries
Because middleware cannot be used with cloud-based systems like Salesforce

Because it concentrates risk (a hub outage affects every connected spoke) and adds infrastructure, latency, and a learning curve that have to be weighed against the N-squared costs of point-to-point at scale
questions.explain: Middleware isn't free: it concentrates risk in the hub, adds a network hop, and requires licensing, configuration, and a learning curve. An architect weighs those real costs against the N-squared costs of point-to-point before choosing it.
